In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[abstract algebra]], a '''signalizer [[functor]]''' is a mapping from a potential [[Subgroup|finite subgroup]] to the [[Centralizer and normalizer|centralizers]] of the nontrivial elements of an [[abelian group]]. The '''signalizer functor theorem''' provides the conditions under which the source of such a functor is in fact a subgroup. 

The signalizer functor was first defined by [[Daniel Gorenstein]].<ref name="gorenstein" /> [[George Glauberman]] proved the Solvable Signalizer Functor Theorem for [[Solvable group|solvable groups]]<ref name="glauberman" /> and Patrick McBride proved it for general groups.<ref name="mcbride-1982a" /><ref name="mcbride-1982b" /> Results concerning signalizer functors play a major role in the [[classification of finite simple groups]].

==Definition==
Let ''A'' be a non-[[Cyclic group|cyclic]] elementary abelian [[P-group|''p''-subgroup]] of the finite group ''G.'' An '''A-signalizer functor on ''G''''' (or simply a '''signalizer functor''' when ''A'' and ''G'' are clear) is a [[Map (mathematics)|mapping]] ''θ'' from the set of nonidentity elements of ''A'' to the set of ''A''-invariant ''p′''-subgroups of ''G'' satisfying the following properties:
*For every nonidentity element <math>a\in A</math>, the group <math>\theta(a) </math> is contained in <math>C_G(a).</math>
*For every pair of nonidentity elements <math>a, b\in A</math>, we have <math>\theta(a) \cap C_G(b) \subseteq \theta(b).</math>

The second condition above is called the '''balance condition.''' If the subgroups <math>\theta(a)</math> are all [[solvable group|solvable]], then the signalizer functor <math>\theta</math> itself is said to be solvable.

==Solvable signalizer functor theorem==
Given <math>\theta,</math> certain additional, relatively mild, assumptions allow one to prove that the subgroup <math>W= \langle \theta(a) \mid a \in  A, a \neq 1\rangle</math> of <math>G</math> generated by the subgroups <math>\theta(a)</math> is in fact a <math>p'</math>-subgroup. 

The Solvable Signalizer Functor Theorem proved by Glauberman states that this will be the case if <math>\theta</math> is solvable and <math>A</math> has at least three generators.<ref name="glauberman"/> The theorem also states that under these assumptions, <math>W</math> itself will be solvable.

Several weaker versions of the theorem were proven before Glauberman's proof was published. Gorenstein proved it under the stronger assumption that <math>A</math> had [[Rank (mathematics)|rank]] at least 5.<ref name="gorenstein"/> [[David Goldschmidt]] proved it under the assumption that <math>A</math> had rank at least 4 or was a 2-group of rank at least 3.<ref name="goldschmidt-1972a"/><ref name="goldschmidt-1972b"/> Helmut Bender gave a simple proof for 2-groups using the [[ZJ theorem]],<ref name="bender"/> and Paul Flavell gave a proof in a similar spirit for all primes.<ref name="flavell"/> Glauberman gave the definitive result for solvable signalizer functors.<ref name="glauberman"/>  Using the classification of finite simple groups, McBride showed that <math>W</math> is a <math>p'</math>-group without the assumption that <math>\theta</math> is solvable.<ref name="mcbride-1982a"/><ref name="mcbride-1982b"/>

===Completeness===
The terminology of completeness is often used in discussions of signalizer functors. Let <math>\theta</math> be a signalizer functor as above, and consider the set И of all <math>A</math>-invariant <math>p'</math>-subgroups <math>H</math> of <math>G</math> satisfying the following condition:
*<math>H\cap C_G(a) \subseteq \theta(a)</math> for all nonidentity <math>a \in A.</math>
For example, the subgroups <math>\theta(a)</math> belong to И as a result of the balance condition of ''θ''. 

The signalizer functor <math>\theta</math> is said to be '''complete''' if И has a unique [[Maximal and minimal elements|maximal element]] when ordered by containment. In this case, the unique maximal element can be shown to coincide with <math>W</math> above, and <math>W</math> is called the '''completion''' of <math>\theta</math>. If <math>\theta</math> is complete, and <math>W</math> turns out to be solvable, then <math>\theta</math> is said to be '''solvably complete.'''

Thus, the Solvable Signalizer Functor Theorem can be rephrased by saying that if <math>A</math> has at least three generators, then every solvable <math>A</math>-signalizer functor on <math>G</math> is solvably complete.

==Examples of signalizer functors==
The easiest way to obtain a signalizer functor is to start with an <math>A</math>-invariant <math>p'</math>-subgroup <math>M</math> of <math>G,</math> and define <math>\theta(a) = M\cap C_G(a)</math> for all nonidentity <math>a \in A.</math> However, it is generally more practical to begin with <math>\theta</math> and use it to construct the <math>A</math>-invariant <math>p'</math>-group.

The simplest signalizer functor used in practice is <math>\theta(a) = O_{p'}(C_G(a)).</math>

As defined above, <math>\theta(a)</math> is indeed an <math>A</math>-invariant <math>p'</math>-subgroup of <math>G</math>, because <math>A</math> is [[abelian group | abelian]]. However, some additional assumptions are needed to show that this <math>\theta</math> satisfies the balance condition. One sufficient criterion is that for each nonidentity <math>a \in A,</math> the group <math>C_G(a)</math> is solvable (or <math>p</math>-solvable or even <math>p</math>-constrained).  

Verifying the balance condition for this <math>\theta</math> under this assumption can be done using [[John G. Thompson|Thompson's]] <math>P\times Q</math>-lemma. 

==Coprime action==
To obtain a better understanding of signalizer functors, it is essential to know the following general fact about finite groups:

*Let <math>E</math> be an abelian  non-cyclic group acting on the finite group <math>X.</math> Assume that the orders of <math>E</math> and <math>X</math> are [[relatively prime]].
*Then <math>X = \langle C_X(E_0) \mid E_0 \subseteq E, \text{ and } E/E_0 \text{ cyclic }\rangle</math>

This fact can be proven using the [[Schur–Zassenhaus theorem]] to show that for each prime <math>q</math> dividing the order of <math>X,</math> the group <math>X</math> has an <math>E</math>-invariant [[Sylow theorems| Sylow <math>q</math>-subgroup]]. This reduces to the case where <math>X</math> is a <math>q</math>-group. Then an argument by [[Mathematical induction| induction]] on the order of <math>X</math> reduces the statement further to the case where <math>X</math> is elementary abelian with <math>E</math> acting  irreducibly. This forces the group <math>E/C_E(X)</math> to be cyclic, and the result follows. <ref name="aschbacher"/><ref name="kurzweil"/>

This fact is used in both the proof and applications of the Solvable Signalizer Functor Theorem.

For example, one useful result is that it implies that if <math>\theta</math> is complete, then its completion is the group <math>W</math> defined above. 

===Normal completion===
Another result that follows from the fact above is that the completion of a signalizer functor is often [[normal subgroup|normal]] in <math>G</math>:

Let <math>\theta</math> be a complete <math>A</math>-signalizer functor on <math>G</math>.

Let <math>B</math> be a noncyclic subgroup of <math>A.</math> Then the coprime action fact together with the balance condition imply that<math>W= \langle \theta(a) \mid a \in  A, a \neq 1\rangle = \langle \theta(b) \mid b \in  B, b \neq 1\rangle. </math>

To see this, observe that because <math>\theta(a)</math> is ''B''-invariant, <math>\theta(a) = \langle \theta(a) \cap C_G(b) \mid b \in B, b \neq 1\rangle \subseteq \langle \theta(b) \mid b \in  B, b \neq 1\rangle.</math> 

The equality above uses the coprime action fact, and the containment uses the balance condition. Now, it is often the case that <math>\theta</math> satisfies an "equivariance" condition, namely that for each <math>g \in G</math> and nonidentity <math>a \in A</math>, <math>\theta(a^g) = \theta(a)^g \, </math> where the superscript denotes conjugation by <math>g.</math> For example, the mapping <math>a \mapsto O_{p'}(C_G(a))</math>, the example of a signalizer functor given above, satisfies this condition.

If <math>\theta</math> satisfies equivariance, ''then the normalizer of <math>B</math> will normalize <math>W.</math>'' It follows that if <math>G</math> is generated by the normalizers of the noncyclic subgroups of <math>A,</math> then the completion of <math>\theta</math> (i.e., ''W'') is normal in <math>G.</math>
